Simon measures the temperature of the tea in his cup, and the thermometer displays a reading of ${59}^{∘}C.$ After $2$ minutes, Simon repeats the measurement and the thermometer displays a reading of  ${51}^{∘}C.$ To the nearest minute, how long does it take for the tea to decrease its temperature to ${26}^{∘}C$ if the temperature in the room is ${12}^{∘}C?$ 

*Hint: You may assume that the temperature $T(t)$ of the tea in Simon's cup decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling, where $T$ is measured in degrees Celsius and $t>0$ is the time, in minutes, since the first measurement.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={12}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-12).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-12} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-12} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-12| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-12>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-12 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-12 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-12 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =12+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature reading was ${59}^{∘}C.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=59,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}59 & =12+K{e}^{0} \\ 59 & =12+K \\ K & =47\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $T(t):$

$$
T(t)=12+47{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $2$ minutes, the thermometer reading is ${51}^{∘}C.$ So, applying the condition $T(2)=51,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}51 & =12+47{e}^{-2k} \\ 39 & =47{e}^{-2k} \\ \frac{39}{47} & ={e}^{-2k} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{39}{47}) & =-2k \\ k & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{39}{47})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the temperature of the tea is ${26}^{∘}C.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =26 \\ 12+47{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =26 \\ 47{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =14 \\ {e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{14}{47} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{14}{47}) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{14}{47}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the tea will have a temperature of ${26}^{∘}C$ after

$$
{t}_{1}=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{14}{47})}{-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{39}{47})}≈13\,\text{min},
$$

rounded to the nearest minute.

$$
\begin{aligned}T-12 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-12 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-12 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =12+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{37}{52} & =\frac{Ke^{-4k}}{Ke^{-1k}} \\ \frac{37}{52} & =e^{-3k} \\ \ln(\frac{37}{52}) & =-3k \\ k & =- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{37}{52} \right)}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now substitute this rate into $T(1)=64$ to determine the constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}52 & =Ke^{-1(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{37}{52} \right)}}{3})} \\ K & =52e^{1(- \frac{\ln{\left(\frac{37}{52} \right)}}{3})} \\ K & =52\left(\frac{52}{37}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

After $15$ minutes, the  temperature of the pork leg is ${100}^{∘}C.$ To the nearest minute, how long does it take for the pork leg to have a temperature of ${60}^{∘}C?$ 

*Hint: You may assume that the temperature reading $T(t)$ of the pork leg decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling, where $T$ is measured in degrees Celsius and $t>0$ is the time, in minutes, since the pork leg was transferred into the ${24}^{∘}C$ room.*

Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={24}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-24).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-24} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-24} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-24| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-24>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-24 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-24 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-24 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =24+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature of the pork leg was ${150}^{∘}C.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=150,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}150 & =24+K{e}^{0} \\ 150 & =24+K \\ K & =126\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $T(t):$

$$
T(t)=24+126{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $15$ minutes, the temperature of the pork leg is ${100}^{∘}C.$ So, applying the condition $T(15)=100,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}100 & =24+126{e}^{-15k} \\ 76 & =126{e}^{-15k} \\ \frac{38}{63} & ={e}^{-15k} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{38}{63}) & =-15k \\ k & =-\frac{1}{15}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{38}{63})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the pork leg has a temperature of ${60}^{∘}C.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =60 \\ 24+126{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =60 \\ 126{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =36 \\ {e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{2}{7} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{7}) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{7}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the pork leg will have a temperature of ${60}^{∘}C$ after

$$
{t}_{1}=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{7})}{-\frac{1}{15}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{38}{63})}≈37\,\text{min},
$$

rounded to the nearest minute.

*Hint: You may assume that the temperature $T(t)$ of the tea in Simon's cup decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling, where $T$ is measured in degrees Celsius and $t>0$ is the time, in minutes, since the first measurement.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={28}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-28).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-28} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-28} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-28| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-28>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-28 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-28 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-28 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =28+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature reading was ${60}^{∘}C.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=60,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}60 & =28+K{e}^{0} \\ 60 & =28+K \\ K & =32\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $T(t):$

$$
T(t)=28+32{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $10$ minutes, the thermometer reading is ${52}^{∘}C.$ So, applying the condition $T(10)=52,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}52 & =28+32{e}^{-10k} \\ 24 & =32{e}^{-10k} \\ \frac{3}{4} & ={e}^{-10k} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{4}) & =-10k \\ k & =-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{4})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when the temperature of the tea is ${40}^{∘}C.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T({t}_{1}) & =40 \\ 28+32{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =40 \\ 32{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =12 \\ {e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =\frac{3}{8} \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{8}) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{8}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the tea will have a temperature of ${40}^{∘}C$ after

$$
{t}_{1}=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{8})}{-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{4})}≈34\,\text{min},
$$

rounded to the nearest minute.
